title: Four initiatives, one that spends what it hasn't budgeted
intro:
*Five minutes. Commit before you look.*

Four AI initiatives an internal communications team could plausibly propose this quarter. All four are real product categories, all four would get funded in most organizations, and none of them is stupid.

**One of them increases the attention bill without anyone deciding that it should.** Find it.

The question isn't which sounds most useful. It is: *after this ships, who decides whether the next message is worth sending?*

artifacts.label: Initiative A · the consolidated digest
artifacts.body: Replace the eleven separate announcements the function currently sends each week with one AI-assembled Friday digest. The model drafts section summaries from the source posts; a communicator edits and approves the whole thing before it goes. Sponsors who want something in it have to make the cut.

artifacts.label: Initiative B · the milestone bot
artifacts.body: Connect an agent to the project tracker. Whenever a project crosses a milestone, it drafts and posts a short announcement to the relevant Slack channel and the company feed: no ticket, no queue, no waiting on comms. "Everyone stays informed automatically, and it costs the team nothing."

artifacts.label: Initiative C · the homepage that knows you
artifacts.body: Personalize the intranet homepage per employee using role, location, and language. The same corpus of content, filtered so a warehouse supervisor in Ohio and a product manager in Dublin each see the four items that actually apply to them, instead of the same undifferentiated forty.

artifacts.label: Initiative D · the pre-send reviewer
artifacts.body: An AI check that runs on every draft before it's sent: flags jargon, unexplained acronyms, reading level above the workforce's median, and any claim that doesn't appear in the source material the drafter attached.

options.label: C — the homepage that knows you

reasoning:
**B is the one, and the tell is who holds the decision afterwards.**

In A, C, and D a human still decides that a given message is worth an audience's time. In B, that decision is transferred to an external system's activity level. Volume becomes a function of how many projects your organization is running and how finely their milestones are configured, not of anyone's judgment about whether the workforce needs to know. Nobody chose to send the four hundredth milestone post. It arrived because a project manager ticked a box in a tracker.

That is Lesson 1's mechanism running in reverse. Writing time used to force somebody to decide the message was worth ninety minutes. B removes the last remaining rationing step and replaces it with a trigger. **An initiative that makes sending free and automatic does not reduce the cost of communication; it removes the last person who was deciding.**

Note also what B does to belief. Each post is individually defensible and collectively corrosive, the channel fills with announcements nobody asked for, and the message that actually matters next month arrives into a feed people have learned to scroll past. You spend attention *and* credit, and the invoice for both lands somewhere you'll never see it.

**A is the strongest of the four**, and it is worth noticing why: it is a *kill list with a schedule attached*. Eleven sends become one, and the scarcity is re-imposed deliberately — sponsors now have to compete for space. That is Module 3's whole argument, arriving early.

**C is targeting**, which is the high-maturity use the benchmark says three-quarters of the profession hasn't reached `[V]`. It reduces the attention bill without reducing what anyone can find. The failure mode to watch is filtering someone out of something they needed, which is a real risk and a solvable one, but it doesn't increase volume.

**D is a quality gate.** It improves what gets sent and is silent on how much. Useful, and not an answer to this module's problem: a clearer message you didn't need to send still costs the same minutes.
